Today it hit home how different living in a small town is compared to a city. No one here is in any kind of hurry, because frankly, there's no real reason to be. We don't have long lines anywhere and there are no traffic tie-ups along the way.

I was helping a customer and it turned into a "lengthy" transaction of maybe 3 or 4 minutes. A woman who just moved here from one of those very busy crowded places back east had come in just as I began helping the first person.

When it was her turn, I said, "Thank you for your patience as you waited." She said, "I was being patient on the outside, but I sure wasn't being on the inside."

In that moment, it occurred to me just how laid back we seem to new-comers. She hasn't learned that 3 or 4 minutes is actually a fairly short transaction because (since she was waiting) the first customer and I didn't engage in normal, polite, small town chit-chat about the weather, or crops, or who is sick or who died last week or how our gardens are doing so far or how the town kids did in little league, etc., etc., etc.

In really thinking about it, I remembered that it took at least three or four years of severe culture shock and decompressing before the feeling that I must hurry all the time gradually eased back. I imagine her culture shock is every bit as intense as mine was years ago. If she sticks it out here, she'll slow down eventually and feel just as patient on the inside as she appeared to be on the outside.

Maybe someday she'll even get to the point of vowing that she won't go back to the city for anything in the world. I know I wouldn't!

Small town life is good.
